title: Philip Neri
hookLine: the laughing saint of Rome, who wore his clothes inside out to stay humble

lines: HALF A BEARD, CLOTHES INSIDE OUT.
cards: A priest is walking through the streets of Rome with half his beard shaved off. Another day, tradition says, he goes out with his clothes on inside out. People stare.
Some laugh. That's the point. This is Philip Neri, and Rome remembers him as the laughing saint.

People came to him for confession and advice, and some hoped to meet a holy man. What they found, the stories say, might be a joke, a silly hat, or a book of funny stories read aloud with a perfectly straight face.
Behind it all sat a serious question: how do you stay humble when people start calling you a saint?

teach.h: A PRIEST WHO TALKED WITH PEOPLE.
teach.b: He lived in Rome in the age of the reformations, when the Catholic Church was working to renew itself from the inside. He didn't lead armies of preachers or write a well-known book.

He talked with people and heard confessions. He gathered young men in a room to pray, read scripture, sing and talk about God, and the community that grew from those meetings came to be called the Oratory.

teach.h: SILLY ON PURPOSE, TO GUARD HUMILITY.
teach.b: Tradition says that when people began treating him as a living saint, he'd do something ridiculous on purpose, so they'd laugh at him instead of praising him. He wasn't mocking holiness. He was guarding it.
The saying linked to him is today's line: cheerfulness strengthens the heart.
It echoes a proverb in the King James Bible: "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones."
And Paul, in his second letter to the Corinthians, says of giving: "for God loveth a cheerful giver."
Seen this way, cheerfulness isn't a mood that shows up when life is easy. It's a strength you can lean on. A heart that can laugh at itself is harder to puff up, and harder to crush.
And if you don't need to look impressive, your attention is free to go to other people. Catholics honor Philip Neri as a saint, and the proverb he echoes sits in the Bible Christians share.

how: Catholics honor Philip Neri as a saint, and the Oratory communities that look back to him still gather for prayer, scripture and music; stories of his humor are often retold on his feast day.

o: an Italian monk who wrote a well-known book of funny stories
a Roman bishop who led preachers against the reformers
a Roman priest who stayed humble by making people laugh

p: half a beard, clothes inside out
silly on purpose, to stay humble
the community that grew around him

s: Philip Neri's jokes made fun of holiness
the stories say he played the fool to guard his own humility, not to mock what was holy.
the line about a merry heart comes from the Bible
it's in Proverbs: a merry heart doeth good like a medicine.
in this lesson, cheerfulness is a mood that only comes when life is easy
it's treated as a strength you can lean on, one that keeps a heart from puffing up or breaking.

games.q: you're Philip Neri. people have started whispering that you're a living saint, and a visitor has come to see the holy man. what do you do?
o: put on your most serious face and give a blessing.
do something ridiculous so they laugh at you instead.
games.why: tradition says he did just that: half a beard, clothes inside out, a funny book read with a straight face. the joke kept the praise from going to his head.

practice: Do one small, humbly silly thing, never at anyone else's expense: hum a tune badly, or read a line aloud in a ridiculous voice, and let yourself smile.
Notice the little voice asking what people would think, and breathe until it gets a little smaller. If you pray, hold the proverb gently: a merry heart doeth good like a medicine.
If not, rest in the lightness of not having to look impressive.

wordCard.voice: Philip Neri. A priest of Rome remembered as the laughing saint, who made himself look silly on purpose to stay humble, and who treated cheerfulness as a strength of the heart.

orig.note: Greek: cheerful, the word Paul uses for the cheerful giver in 2 Corinthians 9:7.

carryVoice: Your line: cheerfulness strengthens the heart. Even a saint can wear his clothes inside out. I'm glad you came.
